blocks.content: The MCP Connector lets you connect MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers directly from the Messages API, without implementing your own MCP client. Claude can use those servers' tools as if they were normal tools.

blocks.title: MCP: the USB-C for AI
blocks.content: MCP is the open standard for connecting AI to external systems: databases, APIs, calendars, Notion, Jira, etc. The MCP Connector is direct access to that ecosystem from the API, without you managing the client.

rows.value: Remote servers with a public URL (HTTPS).
No extra code. Anthropic handles the connection.
Only supports tools (no MCP resources or prompts).
Local servers (stdio), MCP resources, MCP prompts.
Full control. Supports the entire MCP spec.
Requires implementing and managing the client.

items.title: Define the server
items.body: You add the server to the `mcp_servers` array with its URL, name, and optional auth token.

items.title: Configure tools
items.body: In the `tools` array you create an `mcp_toolset` that points to the server. You can enable/disable specific tools.

items.title: Claude uses the tools
items.body: Claude calls the server's tools when the query requires it. Responses arrive as `mcp_tool_result` in the content.

items.title: All tools
items.description: Without `default_config` or `configs`: Claude sees all of the server's tools.

items.title: Denylist
items.description: Enable all by default and disable the dangerous ones (delete, share, etc.) in `configs`.

items.title: Multiple servers
items.description: You can connect several servers in the same request. Each one needs its own `mcp_toolset`.

blocks.title: Requirements
blocks.content: The MCP server must be publicly accessible over HTTPS. Local (stdio) servers can't be used with the MCP Connector. Requires the beta header `anthropic-beta: mcp-client-2025-11-20`.

Extended Thinking lets Claude generate an internal reasoning block before the final response, useful for problems that require several logical steps (math, debugging, planning). It's controlled with a token budget (`budget_tokens`) dedicated exclusively to that reasoning.

rows.value: Direct, with no visible process.
Only input and output tokens.
Simple tasks, fast responses.
Includes `thinking` blocks with the reasoning.
Input + output tokens + thinking tokens.
Math, debugging, deep analysis, complex logic.

blocks.title: Thinking with multi-turn tool use
blocks.content: `budget_tokens` has a minimum of 1024 tokens (the API rejects lower values) and must be less than `max_tokens`. Budgets above 32K generally don't improve quality. In multi-turn conversations with tools, the `thinking` block includes a `signature` that authenticates it and must be forwarded intact inside the `assistant` message. Modifying, truncating, or removing it invalidates the signature and produces an error.

blocks.title: This mode (`type: "enabled"`) is being phased out
blocks.content: This manual form with `budget_tokens` works on Sonnet 4.6, but is already deprecated there, and outright rejected with a 400 error on Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and the entire Claude 5 family (Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Fable 5). The replacement is `thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}`, where Claude decides whether to think and how much based on the request's difficulty, controlling depth with `output_config: {"effort": "low"|"medium"|"high"}` instead of a fixed token budget. It's worth knowing `budget_tokens` because it's taught and tested that way in the CCAR-F exam, but on a new project on an Opus 4.7+ model you should use adaptive mode.

Sometimes Claude's internal reasoning triggers Anthropic's safety systems. Instead of a readable `thinking` block, the response includes a `redacted_thinking` block with the content encrypted in a `data` field — it can't be read, but Claude still needs it to avoid losing context for the rest of the conversation.

blocks.title: Forward it intact, just like a normal thinking block
blocks.content: If your code filters blocks by type before forwarding them in a multi-turn tool-use turn (for example `if block.type == "thinking"`), you also need to include `block.type == "redacted_thinking"` — filtering only on `"thinking"` silently drops these blocks and breaks the multi-turn conversation protocol.

items.title: Use it for
items.description: Math problems, complex debugging, multi-step logical analysis, decisions with many variables.

items.title: Avoid it for
items.description: Simple questions, FAQ chatbots, direct creative generation, when speed is critical.

blocks.content: Claude can receive images (base64-encoded or by URL) alongside text in the same message, and reason about their content: describe them, read text in them, compare charts, analyze UI screenshots. A single message can include several images for comparisons. Supports PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP.

blocks.title: Cost scales with resolution
blocks.content: An image's token consumption grows with its pixel size. For very large screenshots or high-resolution photos where fine detail isn't needed, resizing them before sending reduces cost without losing the relevant information.

Vision isn't infallible by default: on counting or fine-detail tasks, a simple prompt ("how many marbles are there?") fails more often than expected even with a sharp image. The same prompt engineering techniques that work with text — breaking it into steps, asking for verification with a different method, giving a solved example (one-shot) — noticeably improve accuracy on complex visual tasks.

blocks.code:
Analyze this image and determine the exact count using this methodology:
1. Identify each marble one by one, assigning it a number.
2. Verify the result by counting with a different method: starting from
   the bottom left, row by row.

What is the exact, verified number of marbles?

blocks.content: PDFs are sent as a `document` type block. Claude processes them both visually and textually at once: it can read the text, but also see tables, charts, and diagrams within the document, something a plain-text extractor would miss.

By enabling `citations` on a source document, Claude anchors each claim in its response to an exact fragment of the original document, returning verifiable references. It works on PDFs (citing by page) and on plain-text documents (citing by character range). It's especially valuable in RAG: passing each retrieved chunk as an independent document with citations enabled lets the UI show exactly which chunk each sentence came from.

blocks.title: The title field isn't cosmetic
blocks.content: Besides `citations: {"enabled": true}`, it's worth sending `title` in the `document` block — it's the name that will appear identifying the source in each returned citation. Without it, the UI has no way to show the user which document each reference came from when there are several.

Before generating a single word, Claude has to process the entire input: tokenize it, compute each token's internal context relative to the rest of the prompt (attention). Without caching, that work is discarded as soon as the response finishes — and on the next call, even if 90% of the prompt is identical to the previous one (same system prompt, same tools, the entire conversation history repeated word for word), Claude processes it all again from scratch. In a multi-turn conversation, that means reprocessing an ever-longer history on every new message, even though nothing old has changed.

`cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` tells the server: save the result of processing everything up to here. On the next call, if that same content appears again with the breakpoint in the same position, the saved result is read instead of recomputed — which is why a cache read costs a fraction of a normal input. The first write isn't free: it costs somewhat more than a request without caching, because besides processing the content it also has to be persisted. The savings appear starting with the second call that reuses that prefix.

rows: Interactive sessions with frequent turns (each read renews the timer)
Agents with long pauses, scheduled jobs, when the gap between requests exceeds 5 minutes

blocks.title: Exact match, not "similar"
blocks.content: Caching isn't a semantic search and doesn't tolerate changes: if a single character changes anywhere before the breakpoint (or the model is switched), it's a complete cache miss — everything is reprocessed from that point, not just the modified part. That's why breakpoints go on what's literally identical between calls (system prompt, tool definitions), never on content that varies turn to turn.

items.title: Exact prefix
items.description: If a single token changes in the content before the breakpoint, or the model is switched, the result is a complete cache miss, not a partial one.

items.title: Minimum token count
items.description: Below a certain threshold (on the order of thousands of tokens depending on the model), content doesn't get cached.

items.title: Up to 4 breakpoints
items.description: Common practice: one at the end of the tools, another at the end of the system prompt, leaving the conversation tail unmarked (since it changes every turn).

blocks.code:
tools = [weather_tool, calendar_tool]
tools[-1]["cache_control"] = {"type": "ephemeral"}  # breakpoint #1: caches all tools

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=500,
    tools=tools,
    system=[
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": full_internal_documentation,  # several thousand tokens, stable
            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"},  # breakpoint #2: extended TTL
        }
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do I configure rate limiting?"}],
)

# check whether the cache was used
print(response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens, response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)

blocks.title: Don't mutate the original tools
blocks.content: The example above modifies `tools[-1]` directly, which is fine if that list is disposable. But if your tool schemas live in a variable shared across requests (a module-level constant, for example), mutating it in place permanently attaches the `cache_control` to it and can break things if you later reorder or filter the tools. Safer to clone before touching: `tools_clone = [t.copy() for t in tools]; tools_clone[-1] = {**tools_clone[-1], "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}`.

blocks.title: Order matters: tools → system → messages
blocks.content: Internally, Claude always concatenates the request in that order: tools first, then the system prompt, then the messages. A breakpoint caches everything that came before it in that order — not just the block where you placed it. That's why a breakpoint on the last tool caches the tools but not the system prompt, while a breakpoint at the end of the system prompt caches tools + system together. It's best to put breakpoints on the most stable content (tools, then system) and leave the conversation messages unmarked, since they change every turn.

left.head: Antipattern: dynamic content before the breakpoint

rows.value: The current time, the user ID, or the latest conversation turns are interpolated before the static block or before the cache_control breakpoint

Any change there invalidates the cache for everything that follows, including the thousands-of-tokens static block that was actually reusable — you pay the write cost (~1.25x-2x) on every request instead of the ~0.1x of a cache read

right.head: Optimal solution: layer by change frequency

rows.value: The most stable content (tools, long system prompt) comes first with its breakpoint; the variables that change on every request go last, after the final breakpoint
A dynamic variable's change doesn't invalidate anything cached; `cache_read_input_tokens` > 0 consistently on repeated requests

blocks.title: cache_control requires the long form
blocks.content: `"content": "text"` (a plain string) doesn't support `cache_control`. To mark a breakpoint you need the block form: `"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "text", "cache_control": {...}}]`, just like it's done with `system` in the example above.

Read and write aren't mutually exclusive within the same request: if you keep the same tools but change the system prompt, you'll see `cache_read_input_tokens` > 0 (for the tools, which did match) and `cache_creation_input_tokens` > 0 at the same time (for the new system prompt, written from scratch). This is the expected result of having several independent breakpoints, not a bug.
The Files API lets you upload files once and reuse them across multiple requests using a `file_id`. It avoids resending and re-encoding the same document or large image on every API call.

items.title: Upload the file
items.body: You use `POST /v1/files` with the file. The response includes a unique `file_id`.

items.title: Save the file_id
items.body: The `file_id` persists until you delete it. You can reuse it in any future request.

items.title: Reference it in messages
items.body: Instead of sending the full file, you include `{ "type": "file", "file_id": "..." }` in the block's source.

items.title: List files
items.description: `client.beta.files.list()` — returns all files uploaded in your workspace.

items.title: View metadata
items.description: `client.beta.files.retrieve_metadata(file_id)` — name, type, size, and creation date.

items.title: Download
items.description: Only files generated by code execution. Files you uploaded yourself aren't downloadable via the API.

blocks.title: Requirements
blocks.content: Requires the beta header `anthropic-beta: files-api-2025-04-14`. Files are shared across all API keys in the same workspace.

The `code_execution` tool gives Claude an isolated environment (a sandbox managed by Anthropic) where it can run real Python: compute, generate charts with matplotlib, process datasets, create files. It's different from the `bash` tool: if both are used in the same conversation, they're two separate execution environments, with no shared state between them.

rows.value: Python sandbox: compute, chart, analyze data.
Persists across calls within the same conversation.
Text, images (matplotlib), files with file_id.
Full shell: install packages, git, scripts, system commands.
Persistent shell session across commands.
stdout/stderr from the commands.

blocks.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# code_execution: Claude computes and can generate charts
response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=2000,
    tools=[{"type": "code_execution_20250825", "name": "code_execution"}],
    betas=["code-execution-2025-08-25"],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Calculate the mean and standard deviation of [12, 15, 11, 19, 22, 14] and plot a histogram"}],
)

# the response includes "tool_result" blocks with the code's output
# and eventually references to generated files (charts as file_id)

blocks.title: Combine with Files API
blocks.content: The code execution tool and the Files API complement each other: you can upload a CSV dataset with the Files API for code execution to process, and retrieve the generated charts also by file_id. Files generated by code execution are downloadable, unlike the ones you uploaded yourself.

subsections.title: A ready-made agent harness, on Anthropic's infrastructure

blocks.content: So far, everything that runs an agent (the tool-use loop, conversation persistence, the sandbox where bash/code execution run) is built and maintained by your application, request by request. Managed Agents is the alternative: instead of a stateless endpoint you send messages to, it's a stateful API that provides the complete harness — agent loop, sandbox, prompt caching, and compaction already handled by Anthropic — designed for long, asynchronous tasks, not the typical request-response of the Messages API.

rows: Model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, and skills — created once and referenced by id in each session
Where the session runs: an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox, or a self-hosted one on your own infrastructure
A running instance of an agent inside an environment, executing a concrete task
The messages exchanged with the session: user turns, tool results, status updates — via server-sent events

blocks.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

agent = client.beta.agents.create(
    name="Coding assistant",
    model="claude-opus-5",
    system="You are a programming assistant. Write clean, documented code.",
    tools=[{"type": "agent_toolset_20260401"}],  # pre-built tool set: bash, files, web
)

environment = client.beta.environments.create(
    name="my-environment",
    config={"type": "cloud", "networking": {"type": "unrestricted"}},
)

session = client.beta.sessions.create(agent=agent.id, environment_id=environment.id)

with client.beta.sessions.events.stream(session.id) as stream:
    client.beta.sessions.events.send(session.id, events=[
        {"type": "user.message", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Generate the first 20 Fibonacci numbers in fibonacci.txt"}]},
    ])
    for event in stream:
        if event.type == "agent.tool_use":
            print(f"[using tool: {event.name}]")
        elif event.type == "session.status_idle":
            break  # the session is still alive: more events can be sent later

blocks.title: Sessions with real state, not a history you resend yourself
blocks.content: Unlike the manual Messages API loop (where you save and resend the messages array on every request), here the history, the sandbox filesystem, and the results stay persisted server-side. The session can be paused and resumed later, or interrupted mid-execution by sending a new event to redirect the agent — there's no need to rebuild context from scratch.

rows.value: Total: you decide every step of the loop, where each tool runs.
The sandbox, persistence, and scheduling are your responsibility.
Short tasks, request-response, or when you already have your own execution infrastructure.
Delegated: Anthropic runs the loop, you send events and consume them.
Sandbox (cloud or self-hosted), caching, and compaction already handled.
Long tasks (minutes or hours), asynchronous, with multiple tool calls and a need to resume the session later.

blocks.title: Scheduled deployments: the server-side equivalent of a cron
blocks.content: Managed Agents supports running an agent on a recurring schedule (cron) directly on Anthropic's infrastructure, without your own app needing to stay running to trigger it. It's the API version of the autonomous debugging pattern seen in Introduction to Claude Code → Autonomous Debugging: a scheduled agent that monitors something and acts, with no interactive session involved.

blocks.title: Beta, and not eligible for Zero Data Retention
blocks.content: Managed Agents requires the beta header `managed-agents-2026-04-01` and is in beta. Because it's stateful by design (it saves history, sandbox state, and outputs server-side), it isn't eligible for Zero Data Retention or for a HIPAA BAA — unlike the Messages API, where ZDR is an option. Relevant if the project has compliance requirements around data retention.
